description: We are a team from a classical mathematics faculty, combining rigorous fundamental education with modern technologies and a hands-on approach to problem-solving. We are ambitious scientists with a proven track record of victories at space hackathons, eager to apply our mathematical foundation and technical skills to the challenges of space exploration.
summary: A sunlit site near the Moon’s south pole can still lose sight of Earth behind a ridge. Lunar Navigator lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare landing sites and dates by asking how long both the Sun and Earth remain visible above local terrain. For one 62-hour operation, three of seven reference sites meet the same visibility requirement. At one site, widening the allowed start-time variation from 15 to 16 minutes in either direction changes the result for two of 221 combinations of position and terrain model. Users can reproduce the experiment, inspect the local horizon, and export the assumptions behind a candidate schedule.
details:
Lunar Navigator starts with an operational question. Given a date and a required duration, where on the Moon could a surface team keep both the Sun and Earth in view? Users can test a fixed start or search for an interval at seven south-polar reference sites. They choose an observer height of 1, 2, or 5 meters and compare the results across 13 months, from November 2026 through November 2027.

We use NASA lunar elevation data to calculate how high the terrain rises in each direction. We then compare this local horizon with the apparent positions and sizes of the Sun and Earth. A window qualifies when more than half of each disk remains visible simultaneously throughout the requested interval. The detailed Connecting Ridge study uses NASA/JPL Horizons. The seven-site comparison uses ephemerides derived from NASA’s NAIF kernels, with selected directions checked against Horizons. Python scripts prepare and check the data. The JavaScript and WebGL application links the calculation to a timeline, orbital imagery, and a 3D terrain view at two sites.

The film poses a test the viewer can repeat. For 62 hours beginning at 12:10 UTC on 22 November 2026, with the observer 5 meters above the ground, Connecting Ridge 01, Connecting Ridge 06, and the Amundsen Rim reference point qualify on their nominal terrain models. At Connecting Ridge 01, we repeat the test at 17 positions on 13 terrain surfaces. All 221 combinations qualify for every start within ±15 minutes. At ±16 minutes, 219 qualify. One case loses coverage at the beginning of the operation and another at the end.

A planner can try another start time while keeping the required duration, then export a scenario card with the UTC interval, terrain source, and assumptions. An educator can hold the site fixed and change the date to show how the horizon affects visibility. Users can also enter their own coordinates for a comparison on a reference sphere. The results quantify geometric visibility. Assessing available electrical power, radio-link performance, or landing safety requires additional engineering models. The animated descent illustrates the terrain.

We used ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex to explore design alternatives, locate and interpret scientific documentation, write and debug code, check numerical results, edit English text, and coordinate team reviews. Codex also assisted with interface design, captions, and film composition. Kokoro-82M generated the English narration. We synthesized the original instrumental score with code developed using Codex. The Earth visualization adapts the day and night rendering approach from our earlier SafeSatelleS application. The planner calculates visibility from the credited lunar elevations and ephemerides.
